extracted.intended_audience: Worldcon members, science fiction & fantasy authors and fans, and general readers interested in Hugo Award rules and history
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of the Hugo Awards' procedures, eligibility, category definitions, and voting system as described on the Wikipedia page. Covers nomination and voting rules, category word-count/format definitions, and special/retro award provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work eligibility (publication/translation timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Works are eligible for an award if they were published or first translated into English in the prior calendar year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are no written rules as to which works qualify as science fiction or fantasy, and the decision of eligibility in that regard is left up to the voters, rather than to the organizing committee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may nominate and nomination timeframe
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the current or previous year's Worldcon are allowed to submit a nomination ballot of works from January through March of each year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nominators are limited to five nominations per category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of nominations per nominator
rubrics_metrics.description: Each nominator may list up to five works in each category on their nomination ballot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This five-per-category limit applies during the January–March nomination window.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finalist list creation (E Pluribus Hugo)
rubrics_metrics.description: The nominations are used to make the list of six finalists per category using a custom-designed voting system known as E Pluribus Hugo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E Pluribus Hugo is a proportional/nominating voting system in which nominees are eliminated one by one and votes for eliminated works are redistributed to the uneliminated works they nominated, intended to ensure that organised minority groups cannot dominate every finalist position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final ballot size (current)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final ballot contains six finalists in each category (changed from five prior to 2017).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior to 2017 the final ballot was five works in each category; the final ballot size was increased to six when E Pluribus Hugo rules were ratified for use beginning in 2017.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on multiple finalists by same author/group/series
rubrics_metrics.description: No more than two works by a given author or group, or in the same dramatic series, can be in one category on the final ballot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page also states 'Finalists are also restricted to two finalists by each author in each category' as part of the post-2015/2016 reforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for finalists appearance threshold (removed)
rubrics_metrics.description: A previous rule that mandated finalists must appear on at least five percent of ballots was eliminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This elimination was part of the changes accompanying E Pluribus Hugo to allow categories to reach a full set of finalists even when the initial pool is very large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may vote and voting timeframe
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the current year's Worldcon then rank the finalists in each category in a vote held roughly from April through July (subject to change depending on when that year's Worldcon is held).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voting access is tied to Worldcon membership for the year of the awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voting method: instant-runoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Votes are counted using instant-runoff voting to determine the winner in each category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the method used on the final ranked ballot to select winners after the finalist list is set.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Award option
rubrics_metrics.description: Voters may also vote for 'no award' in any category, indicating that they feel that any finalists ranked below it are not worthy of a Hugo in that category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically 'No Award' has sometimes placed above finalists (including multiple occurrences in the 1950s and in 2015–2016 controversies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre qualification left to voters
rubrics_metrics.description: There are no written rules as to which works qualify as science fiction or fantasy, and the decision of eligibility in that regard is left up to the voters, rather than to the organizing committee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This means classification of borderline works is determined by the electorate, not a central committee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worldcon authority over categories and additional awards
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual Worldcon committees may create additional categories; such additional awards are officially designated as Hugo Awards for that convention but are not required to be repeated by future conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically the number of additional categories allowed has changed (e.g., up to two in 1964, later adjustments), and some special Hugo Awards have been given temporarily without becoming permanent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories may be changed by WSFS
rubrics_metrics.description: The WSFS (World Science Fiction Society) constitution/guidelines have specified categories to be awarded and historically stated those categories could only be changed by the WSFS board/business meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The WSFS business process (meetings and constitution) governs ratification and permanent changes to category structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retro-Hugos eligibility and optional nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Retroactive Hugo Awards (Retro-Hugos) were awarded for years 50, 75, or 100 years earlier in which a Worldcon was held but no Hugos were awarded; in 2017 eligibility was expanded to include years after 1939 in which no Worldcon was held.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retro-Hugos were optional — some Worldcons chose not to award them — and the WSFS constitution was amended in 2025 to remove Retro-Hugos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special (non-voted) awards given by Worldcon committees
rubrics_metrics.description: Worldcon committees may give out special awards during the Hugo ceremony which are not voted on and are not officially Hugo Awards (though they once used the same trophy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two additional awards (Astounding Award for Best New Writer and the Lodestar Award) are presented at the Hugo ceremony and voted on by the same process but are not formally Hugo Awards; other special awards are purely committee-decided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Novel — category definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories of 40,000 words or more
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category start year listed as 1953.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Novella — category definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories of between 17,500 and 40,000 words
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category start year listed as 1968.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Novelette — category definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories of between 7,500 and 17,500 words
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category start year listed as 1955.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Short Story — category definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories of less than 7,500 words
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category start year listed as 1955.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Series — category definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Series of works
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Added as permanent category in 2018 after being run as a special Hugo prior to ratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Related Work — category definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Works which are either non-fiction or noteworthy for reasons other than the fictional text
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category start year listed as 1980 (originally Best Non-Fiction Book).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Graphic Story or Comic — category definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories told in graphic form. (Award was named 'Best Graphic Story' prior to 2020.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category start year listed as 2009.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Dramatic Presentation (Long and Short Forms) — category definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatized productions, divided since 2003 between works longer or shorter than 90 minutes
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category start year listed as 1958; split into Long and Short Form in 2003.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Semiprozine — category definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Semi-professional magazines
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category start year listed as 1984.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Fanzine — category definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-professional magazines
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category start year listed as 1955.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Professional Editor (Long and Short Forms) — category definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors of written works, divided since 2007 between editors of novels (Long Form) or editors of magazines and anthologies (Short Form)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category (as Professional Editor) begins 1973 as replacement for Best Professional Magazine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Professional Artist — category definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional artists
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category start year listed as 1953.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Fan Artist — category definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Fan artists
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category start year listed as 1967.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Fan Writer — category definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Fan writers
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category start year listed as 1967.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Fancast — category definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiovisual fanzines
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category start year listed as 2012.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best Game or Interactive Work — category definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Games (video or tabletop) and interactive fiction
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduced as a special Hugo in 2021 and ratified as a permanent category beginning in 2024 (listed with year 2021 in the table).

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/temporary categories and rolling changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Over the years various categories have been added, split, removed, run as specials, or discontinued (examples: Best Professional Magazine, Best Original Art Work, Best Web Site, Best Art Book, Best Game as special before ratification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Worldcon committees and WSFS business meetings have governed temporary vs permanent status; some categories have been trialed as specials before being made permanent or dropped.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trophy and non-monetary nature of award
rubrics_metrics.description: Winners receive a trophy consisting of a stylized rocket ship on a base; there is no monetary or other remuneration associated with the Hugo other than the trophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rocket shape has been consistent since 1984 though the base design changes each year; the original 1953 design was based on hood ornaments of 1950s cars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy response to bloc voting and slate campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Following organised slate campaigns in 2015–2016, rules (E Pluribus Hugo) were passed to modify the nominations process to reduce the ability of organised minority groups to dominate finalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific changes included the adoption of the E Pluribus Hugo elimination/redistribution method, increasing final ballot size to six, and adjusting thresholds and per-author finalist limits.
